claim: Traffic signals adapt by implementing a 'market-based' system where intersections compete for traffic flow by adjusting their timing to be more accommodating
mechanism: Each intersection operates with a 'budget' of timing flexibility. When an intersection detects higher traffic flow, it can 'spend' some of its budget to increase green time for that approach. However, the budget is replenished based on how efficiently the intersection processes traffic (vehicles per green cycle). This creates a competitive system where intersections that handle traffic more efficiently get more resources to further improve
evidence: Myxomycetes allocate resources based on flow efficiency
Market-based approaches have been successful in other resource allocation problems
assumptions: Traffic efficiency can be accurately measured at each intersection
A budget system can effectively distribute timing resources
Intersections will compete in a way that benefits the overall network
expected_failure_modes: Resource hoarding by already efficient intersections
Inability to respond to sudden changes in traffic patterns
Complexity of the budget system making it difficult to implement and maintain
novelty_rationale: This hypothesis introduces a resource allocation metaphor to the traffic signal problem, where timing flexibility is treated as a scarce resource that is distributed based on performance
testability: Can be tested by implementing the budget system and measuring whether intersections with better performance metrics actually receive more timing flexibility
falsifier: If implementing this budget system leads to some intersections hoarding timing resources while others become chronically under-resourced, creating inequality in the network
